value.overview: The Red-capped Manakin is a small forest bird of the tropical Americas and a member of the manakin family, Pipridae. Adult males are strikingly colored, with a scarlet-red crown and nape, mostly black plumage, and yellow thighs. Females and immature birds are mainly olive green. The species is especially noted for the male’s rapid courtship displays, performed at traditional gathering sites called leks.
value.classification: The Red-capped Manakin belongs to the family Pipridae in the order Passeriformes. Its scientific name is Ceratopipra mentalis; two commonly recognized regional forms occur across its range, including populations in Costa Rica.
value.identification: This small, compact manakin is about 10 centimeters long. The adult male has a bright red crown, forehead, and nape, a black body, yellow thighs, a pale yellow chin, and pale wing linings. The female is dull olive green above with lighter, yellowish-green underparts. Males also have conspicuously pale or whitish irises. Females and immature birds can be difficult to distinguish from other green manakins without close views of range, bill, eye, and plumage details.
value.rangeHabitat: The Red-capped Manakin ranges from southeastern Mexico through Central America to western South America, including parts of Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru. In Costa Rica it is a common resident of lowland forest on the Caribbean slope and in southern Pacific lowlands, extending north on the Pacific side at least to Manuel Antonio National Park. It occurs mainly in humid mature forest, tall second growth, shaded clearings, forest edges, and fruiting trees, generally at low and middle elevations but locally up to about 1,050 meters.
value.migrationStatus: It is primarily resident in Costa Rica and is not a regular long-distance migrant. Local or seasonal movements may occur when birds track changing fruit supplies; increased captures at La Selva in eastern Costa Rica during January and February suggest such movements.
value.breeding: Males gather at traditional leks, where they defend small display areas and perform rapid shuffling, wing, and jumping movements to attract females. Males provide no parental care. The female builds the small nest, incubates the eggs, and raises the young alone. Breeding information varies geographically, but nesting in Costa Rica is associated with humid forest and forest-edge environments, and courtship displays may be observed at fixed sites during the breeding season.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fruits and berries, especially those produced by shrubs and trees in forest understory, gaps, and edges. A Costa Rican study found seeds from many plant species in droppings, including members of the genera Clidemia, Hampea, Henriettea, Miconia, Ossaea, Pinzona, and Psychotria. The species also takes insects and other small arthropods, particularly when feeding requirements increase during breeding.
value.behavior: Red-capped Manakins are usually encountered singly while moving through low and middle forest levels in search of fruit. Males become more conspicuous during courtship, gathering at leks and repeating distinctive displays from thin branches or occasionally near the ground. Outside courtship they are generally quiet and unobtrusive. Their fruit-eating behavior makes them potential dispersers of seeds between forest patches.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and is not currently considered threatened.
